text: That player is often Raphinha. Eleven goals in seven competitive matches is an astonishing return. But put the number aside for a moment and watch the movement. Against Feyenoord, his second goal comes from Pedri threading the ball into his run through the middle. The decisive action begins before the finish. A runner sees a gap. A midfielder sees the same gap. The pass arrives while the defence is still adjusting. That is the relationship opponents have to break. You cannot watch the ball, track every run, and close every passing lane with the same defender. Against Racing, Raphinha scored a hat-trick, including two penalties. So this is not a claim that every goal comes from some unstoppable open-play move. It is a broader problem: Barcelona are reaching dangerous areas in several ways, and Raphinha is turning those moments into punishment. Now look at the players making those moments possible.
